blocks.text: The **Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC)** is a **wholly owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India**. It was set up on **15 July 1978** under the **DICGC Act, 1961**. Its two jobs: insure the deposits that customers keep with banks, and guarantee credit facilities given by banks.

blocks.title: Title of the Act changed
blocks.text: When DIC and CGCI merged in 1978, the Deposit Insurance Act, 1961 was renamed the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961, even though the year 1961 stayed.

blocks.title: DICGC: what the letters hold
blocks.phrase: Deposit Insurance + Credit Guarantee: D-I protects your Deposit, C-G Guards your Credit (loan).
blocks.note: Act year is 1961; DICGC itself dates from 1978. Keep ‘61 for the Act and ‘78 for the Corporation.

sections.title: History: from Bengal crisis to DICGC

blocks.title: How deposit insurance developed in India
items: The idea of insuring bank deposits gets attention for the first time, after the banking crises in Bengal.
The idea is reconsidered but kept in abeyance until the RBI makes adequate arrangements for inspection of banks.
The Rural Banking Enquiry Committee supports deposit insurance.
The failure of the Palai Central Bank Ltd. and the Laxmi Bank Ltd. makes the RBI and the Government think seriously about it.
The Deposit Insurance Corporation (DIC) Bill is introduced in Parliament.
The Bill receives the President’s assent.
The Deposit Insurance Act, 1961 comes into force.
RBI promotes the Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. (CGCI), a public limited company.
DIC and CGCI are merged into the present DICGC.

blocks.title: Early scope of the scheme
items: Deposit insurance was first extended only to functioning **commercial banks**, including the State Bank of India and its subsidiaries, other commercial banks and branches of foreign banks operating in India.

The CGCI’s credit guarantee schemes aimed to encourage commercial banks to lend to neglected sectors, particularly weaker sections engaged in non-industrial activities, by guaranteeing loans to small and needy priority sector borrowers.

blocks.title: Where did the idea start?
blocks.text: Deposit insurance was first discussed in 1948 after the banking crisis in **Bengal**. The Rural Banking Enquiry Committee backed it in 1950. Remember Bengal, not Kerala or Maharashtra.

blocks.title: Dates to know: 48, 50, 60, 61, 71, 78
blocks.phrase: Bengal’s crash in ’48, Rural panel ’50, Palai & Laxmi crash ’60, Act ’61, CGCI ’71, DICGC ’78.
letters: Bengal banking crisis; idea of deposit insurance
Rural Banking Enquiry Committee supports it

blocks.note: The Act year is 1961 but it came into force on 1 January 1962.

sections.title: Insurance cover and how it grew

blocks.text: Under Section 16(1) of the DICGC Act, the insurance cover originally stood at just **₹1,500** per depositor for deposits held in the **same right and same capacity** in all branches of a bank taken together. The Act lets the Corporation raise the limit with the prior approval of the Central Government, and it has done so several times.

blocks.title: Deposit insurance limit over the years
The ₹5 lakh cover
items: The limit of ₹1 lakh had lasted from May 1993; the Damodaran Committee on Customer Services in Banks (2011) had recommended a five-time increase to ₹5 lakh because incomes and individual deposits were rising.
In February 2020, as per the budget provision, DICGC raised the cover from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh per depositor.
The ₹5 lakh cap includes both **principal and interest**.
If a bank goes into liquidation, depositors get insurance money according to their deposits, up to a maximum of ₹5 lakh.
The demand for a higher cover grew stronger after the collapse of the Punjab and Maharashtra Co-operative (PMC) Bank.

blocks.title: Same right, same capacity
blocks.text: The cover is per depositor per bank for deposits held in the same right and capacity, taken across all branches of that bank together. A depositor with accounts in different banks gets cover from each bank separately.

blocks.title: Later update
blocks.text: After the period covered here, a 2021 amendment to the DICGC Act allowed the insured amount (up to the limit) to be paid to depositors within 90 days of a bank being placed under restrictions. Always check the latest rules before an exam.

blocks.title: Limit ladder: 1.5-5-10-20-30 then 1 and 5
blocks.phrase: Years 68, 70, 76, 80 give 5, 10, 20, 30 thousand; 1993 gives 1 lakh; 2020 gives 5 lakh.

blocks.title: Five lakh story
blocks.phrase: PMC crash made people shout; Damodaran asked for 5 times, the budget gave 5 lakh in February 2020.
letters: PMC Bank collapse raised the demand
Damodaran Committee recommended a five-time increase

blocks.title: Banks covered by the Deposit Insurance Scheme
items: All **commercial banks**, including branches of foreign banks functioning in India, **Local Area Banks** and **Regional Rural Banks**.

All eligible **co-operative banks** as defined in Section 2(gg) of the DICGC Act: State, Central and Primary co-operative banks in States and Union Territories that have amended their Co-operative Societies Act as the DICGC Act requires. At the time of writing, all co-operative banks are covered.
Primary co-operative **societies** are not insured by DICGC.

blocks.text: Banks, including regional rural banks, local area banks, foreign banks with branches in India and co-operative banks, are **mandated** to take deposit insurance cover from DICGC. The Union Territories of Lakshadweep and Dadra and Nagar Haveli do not have co-operative banks.

blocks.title: Deposits that are NOT covered
items: Deposits of foreign Governments.
Deposits of Central and State Governments.
Inter-bank deposits.
Deposits of State Land Development Banks with the State co-operative banks.
Any amount due on account of, and deposits received, outside India.
Any amount specifically exempted by the Corporation with the previous approval of the RBI.

blocks.title: Principal plus interest
blocks.text: Insurance covers both the principal and the interest on deposits, but the total payout for a depositor in one bank is capped at ₹5 lakh.

blocks.title: Covered deposits: SFCR
blocks.phrase: SFCR: Savings, Fixed, Current, Recurring all get covered.

blocks.title: Excluded deposits: FIG LOE
blocks.phrase: A FIG LOE (low) is not insured: Foreign govt, Inter-bank, Government (Centre/State), Land development banks, Overseas, Exempted.
letters: State Land Development Banks’ deposits with State co-operative banks
Amounts Exempted by the Corporation with RBI approval

sections.title: Premium and registration of insured banks

blocks.title: Premium rules
items: As per the book, DICGC charges **10 paise per ₹100** of deposits held by a bank. This rate has been revised upwards since, so check the current rate before an exam.
The premium is paid by the **insured bank**, not the customer, and the bank may not pass it on to depositors.
So the benefit of deposit insurance reaches depositors **free of cost**.
The insured bank has to remit the premium half-yearly, by the end of May and the end of November each year.

blocks.title: Registration of an insured bank
items: A bank that fails to pay the premium for **three consecutive half-year periods** can have its registration cancelled by the Corporation.
The bank may later ask for its registration to be restored.
The Corporation can restore it if the bank pays all premium due from the date of default, together with interest.

blocks.title: Who pays the premium?
blocks.text: Not the customer, not the RBI, not the nominee. The **insured bank** pays the premium to DICGC.

blocks.title: Premium in a nutshell
blocks.phrase: Bank pays, depositor stays free; May and November are the dates; three missed half-years and you are out.
letters: Pays the premium, cannot pass it on
Consecutive half-years of default before cancellation

blocks.title: Management of DICGC
rows: ₹50 crore, fully issued and subscribed by the Reserve Bank of India
Manages the Corporation; a Deputy Governor of the RBI is the Chairman
In overall charge of day-to-day operations
Four: Accounts, Deposit Insurance, Credit Guarantee and Administration

blocks.text: The Administration Department looks after staff and establishment matters. Employees of the Corporation are RBI employees, and DICGC is treated as an independent salary-drawing unit.

blocks.title: Two numbers
blocks.text: Authorised capital: ₹50 crore, all subscribed by the RBI. Board chairman: a Deputy Governor of the RBI.

blocks.title: Four departments: A-D-C-A
blocks.phrase: A DC A: Accounts, Deposit Insurance, Credit Guarantee, Administration.

blocks.title: Three funds: DCG
blocks.phrase: DCG: Deposit Insurance Fund, Credit Guarantee Fund, General Fund. The first two are fed by premium and fees; the General Fund pays the bills.

revision: DICGC is a wholly owned subsidiary of the RBI, set up on 15 July 1978 under the DICGC Act, 1961; head office in Mumbai.
DICGC was formed by merging the Deposit Insurance Corporation (DIC) and the Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. (CGCI, promoted 14 January 1971).
The idea of deposit insurance first arose in 1948 after the Bengal banking crisis; the Rural Banking Enquiry Committee supported it in 1950.
The crash of the Palai Central Bank and Laxmi Bank in 1960 pushed the Government towards deposit insurance.
The Deposit Insurance Act, 1961 came into force on 1 January 1962 and the Bill was introduced on 21 August 1961.
The ₹5 lakh cap covers principal plus interest per depositor in one bank, in the same right and capacity.
The demand for a higher cover grew after the PMC Bank collapse; the Damodaran Committee (2011) had asked for a five-time increase.
Covered deposits: savings, fixed, current and recurring. Not covered: foreign governments, Central and State Governments, inter-bank and deposits received outside India.
Commercial banks, local area banks, RRBs, foreign bank branches and co-operative banks are covered; primary co-operative societies are not.
The premium is paid by the insured bank, not the depositor; the book gives the rate as 10 paise per ₹100 of deposits.
Registration can be cancelled if premium is unpaid for three consecutive half-years, and restored on payment of dues with interest.
Authorised capital is ₹50 crore, fully subscribed by the RBI; a Deputy Governor of the RBI chairs the Board.
Four departments: Accounts, Deposit Insurance, Credit Guarantee and Administration; funds: Deposit Insurance, Credit Guarantee and General.
